newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish 97 C/A gap seen at 3-3.5 pct of GDP-fin min.
newsitem.headline: Polish 97 C/A gap seen at 3-3.5 pct of GDP-fin min.

text.p: Poland's current account deficit is likely to rise to 3-3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from 0.75 percent in 1996, Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday.

Belka told journalists that despite the expected rise, the ratio would still remain within acceptable limits, especially compared with much higher current account deficits run up by other countries in central and eastern Europe.
"This is not a problem which should set off alarm bells, but it means that it is better to start doing something about it rather than ignore it," Belka said.
Poland had a current account deficit of $1.35 billion in 1996 against a $5.46 billion surplus in 1995 after imports rose more than 30 percent last year while exports rose only seven percent.

Belka said that the deficit was the reason why Poland would likely delay slowing the zloty's monthly devaluation rate and cutting interest rates, even though consumer and producer price growth was slower than expected.

"(the policies of high real interest rates and not slowing the zloty's devaluation) is an attempt to calm down the economy (and curb) certain elements of global demand to moderate the growth rate of imports," he said.
"A slightly tougher monetary policy will also make sales on the domestic market more attractive than exports," Belka said.
Belka added that depite the current account problems, Poland's economy was in a very good shape.
"The macro-economic picture is very good indeed," he said.
